Appamattuck

Library of Virginia’s biography of Opossunoquonuske introduces leadership and colonial encounters in the Appamattuck towns near the lower Appomattox River. A short DHR account supplies named-place context. These historical readings do not establish a present government or ancestry boundary.

Conjurer’s Field landscape, May 6, 2017
Nyttend, May 6, 2017; via Wikimedia Commons; copyright holder’s explicit worldwide public-domain release.

Source & image record ↗ · Public domain — copyright holder’s explicit worldwide release with fallback grant

The exact file page identifies this dated lawn-and-river view as Conjurer’s Field. DHR’s short marker account places an Appamattuck settlement in the general Conjurer’s Neck area by about 1600; its register description links the two place labels. A modern historical-place landscape, not an original village reconstruction, all-community portrait, earlier-occupation identity assignment, boundary, current ownership claim or invitation to enter. No precise coordinates, road directions, site identifier or private access details are reproduced. The complete delivered frame shows grass, rail fence, river and trees; no people, isolated artwork, remains or ceremony are visible. The exact media rights are Nyttend’s worldwide public-domain release and stated fallback grant, not metadata CC0 or blanket agency status. The normally offered 960 × 638 provider preview was inspected and is preserved unchanged; the 6016 × 4000 original was not inspected. CSS crops and overlays affect display only.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

A named woman’s leadership in colonial accounts

Library of Virginia identifies Opossunoquonuske as a weroansqua leading one Appamattuck town near the Appomattox River’s mouth. Its biography follows an encounter with Newport’s party in 1607 and reports violence and English attacks on Appamattuck towns in 1610–1611. This is an institutional account mediated by colonial descriptions, not a complete community history or a basis for treating one leader’s story as everyone’s experience.

Read the sources [1] Library of Virginia, Virginia Changemakers

02

A named landscape without a territorial claim

DHR’s short Conjurer’s Neck marker account places an Appamattuck settlement in that general Appomattox River area by about 1600. Its mention of much earlier Indigenous occupation does not establish that every archaeological period belongs to the same named community. The place reference supplies local context, not a complete historical boundary, present ownership or visitor access.

Read the sources [2] Virginia Department of Historic Resources

Opossunoquonuske — Virginia Women in History biography ↗

Publication: 2007 Virginia Women in History honoree biography; web publication/update date not stated

A library biography presents one woman’s leadership and the colonial encounters recorded around her town. English-mediated descriptions require critical attribution.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual occupation/biography paragraphs identifying her as a weroansqua of one Appamattuck town, the 1607 encounter and reported 1610–1611 violence; 2007 programme attribution read.

Review recorded: November 3, 2026

Access note: Normal reader and one HTTPS 200 HTML cache. Selected text only. Appearance judgments, attire/ceremonial detail, military totals, underlying original accounts, images and coordinates excluded. Violence is attributed to the biography, not generalized to every Appamattuck community; removal is not extinction or a present membership determination.
